source.title: Selected Open Problems in Continuous-Time Quantum Walks

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with adjacency matrix A and transition matrix U(t)=exp(itA). Suppose G admits perfect state transfer between two vertices, meaning that for some time t and some unit-modulus complex number γ one has U(t)e_u = γ e_v. If G has m edges and diameter D, prove an asymptotic lower bound on m that is stronger than the currently known cubic bound by showing that m belongs to Ω(D^k) for some exponent k>3.
accepted.context_brief: Perfect state transfer edge-vs-diameter lower bounds

evidence.quote: Formally, perfect state transfer occurs at a G between vertices u and v at time t if there is a complex number γ of absolute value 1 so that U(t)e_u = γ e_v.
If perfect state transfer occurs in a graph with m edges of diameter D, show that m in Ω(D^k), for k>3.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with adjacency matrix A and transition matrix U(t)=exp(itA). Find an infinite family of graphs that admit perfect state transfer between some pair of vertices, where perfect state transfer means that U(t)e_u = γ e_v for some time t and unit complex number γ, and such that the size of each graph is bounded above by a polynomial in its diameter.
accepted.context_brief: Polynomial-size families with perfect state transfer

evidence.quote: Formally, perfect state transfer occurs at a G between vertices u and v at time t if there is a complex number γ of absolute value 1 so that U(t)e_u = γ e_v.
Find an infinite family of graphs for which there is perfect state transfer, and the size of the graph is bounded by a polynomial in the diameter.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with adjacency matrix A. Pretty good state transfer between vertices u and v means that there exists a sequence of times t_j for which |exp(i t_j A)_{uv}| tends to 1. Find a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether pretty good state transfer occurs in a given graph, and also give an algorithm that computes a subsequence of times witnessing that convergence.
accepted.context_brief: Algorithms for pretty good state transfer

evidence.quote: there could be distinct values of t for which the sequence (|exp(it_j A)_{uv}|)_{j\ge 0} converges to 1. When this occurs, we say that pretty good state transfer happens in G between u and v.
Find a polynomial time algorithm to test whether pretty good state transfer occurs, and find an algorithm to compute a subsequence of times which represent pretty good state transfer.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with adjacency matrix A and transition matrix U(t)=exp(itA). Say that G admits instantaneous uniform mixing at time τ if all entries of U(τ) have the same absolute value, equivalently if all entries of the mixing matrix M(τ)=U(τ)∘U(-τ) are equal. Prove that whenever G admits uniform mixing at time τ, every eigenvalue of U(τ) is a root of unity.
accepted.context_brief: Uniform mixing and roots of unity

evidence.quote: We say that G admits instantaneous uniform mixing (or simply uniform mixing) at time τ if all entries of M(τ) are equal. Equivalently, G admits uniform mixing at time τ if all entries of U(τ) have the same absolute value.
If G admits uniform mixing at time τ, then the eigenvalues of U(τ) are roots of unity.

accepted.question_text: For the cycle graph C_9 on nine vertices, determine whether its continuous-time quantum walk admits instantaneous uniform mixing, meaning a time τ at which all entries of the transition matrix U(τ) have the same absolute value (equivalently, all entries of M(τ)=U(τ)∘U(-τ) are equal).

evidence.quote: We say that G admits instantaneous uniform mixing (or simply uniform mixing) at time τ if all entries of M(τ) are equal. Equivalently, G admits uniform mixing at time τ if all entries of U(τ) have the same absolute value.
Determine if C_9 admits uniform mixing.

accepted.question_text: Given a graph G together with its eigenvalues and eigenspaces, find necessary and sufficient conditions for the continuous-time quantum walk on G to admit instantaneous uniform mixing, that is, for there to exist a time τ such that all entries of U(τ) have the same absolute value, equivalently all entries of M(τ)=U(τ)∘U(-τ) are equal.

evidence.quote: We say that G admits instantaneous uniform mixing (or simply uniform mixing) at time τ if all entries of M(τ) are equal. Equivalently, G admits uniform mixing at time τ if all entries of U(τ) have the same absolute value.
Given the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of a graph, give necessary and sufficient conditions for uniform mixing to occur.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with adjacency matrix A(G)=Σ_r θ_r E_r, and let its average mixing matrix be \hat{M}=lim_{T→∞}(1/T)∫_0^T M(t)dt = Σ_r E_r∘E_r, where M(t)=U(t)∘U(-t) and U(t)=exp(itA). For a primitive distance-regular graph G, prove that the rank of \hat{M} equals the number of vertices of G.
accepted.context_brief: Rank of average mixing matrix in primitive distance-regular graphs

evidence.quote: The average mixing matrix is defined as \hat{M}=\lim_{T	o\infty}\hat{M}_{[0,T]}, and a straightforward calculation shows that if A(G)=\sum_{r=0}^{d}	heta_r E_r then \hat{M}=\sum_{r=0}^{d} E_r\circ E_r.
If G is a primitive distance-regular graph, show that the rank of \hat{M} is equal to the number of vertices.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with average mixing matrix \hat{M}=lim_{T→∞}(1/T)∫_0^T M(t)dt = Σ_r E_r∘E_r. The non-negative rank of a non-negative n×n matrix is the least k for which the matrix factors through non-negative vectors of dimension k. Determine exactly when the non-negative rank of \hat{M} is equal to n, the number of vertices of G.
accepted.context_brief: Non-negative rank of the average mixing matrix

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with average mixing matrix \hat{M}=lim_{T→∞}(1/T)∫_0^T M(t)dt = Σ_r E_r∘E_r. The completely positive semidefinite rank (cpsd-rank) of \hat{M} is the smallest matrix dimension d for which \hat{M} can be realized as a Gram matrix of positive semidefinite d×d matrices. Compute the cpsd-rank of \hat{M}.

Compute the cpsd-rank of \hat{M}.

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with average mixing matrix \hat{M}. In the extremal cases where either the non-negative rank of \hat{M} or the completely positive semidefinite rank of \hat{M} attains its boundary behavior, determine what combinatorial consequences for G can be deduced from those extremal rank values.
accepted.context_brief: Combinatorial consequences of extremal factorization ranks

evidence.quote: The non-negative rank of a non-negative n	imes n matrix M is the least number k... The completely positive semidefinite rank (cpsd-rank) of a completely positive semidefinite matrix M is the smallest dimension d...
In the extremal cases for the non-negative or cpsd ranks, what combinatorial consequences may be derived?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a graph with average mixing matrix \hat{M}. The completely positive rank (cp-rank) of a completely positive matrix is the smallest dimension d for which the matrix is a Gram matrix of non-negative vectors in R^d. Determine exactly when the cp-rank of \hat{M} is equal to n, the number of vertices of G.
accepted.context_brief: CP-rank of the average mixing matrix

evidence.quote: The completely positive rank (cp-rank) of a completely positive matrix M is the smallest dimension d for which M is a Gram matrix of non-negative vectors in R^d.
When is the cp-rank of \hat{M} is equal to n?

accepted.question_text: Let R be a real-valued random variable with probability density f_R(t), and define the R-averaged mixing matrix by \hat{M}_R = E[M(R)] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} M(t) f_R(t) dt, where M(t)=U(t)∘U(-t) is the mixing matrix of a continuous-time quantum walk. Develop a spectral graph theory for the matrix \hat{M}_R as R varies over probability distributions.
accepted.context_brief: Spectral theory for alternative averaged mixing matrices

evidence.quote: If R is a random variable with probability density function f_R(t)... \hat{M}_R := E[M(R)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} M(t) f_R(t) dt.
Develop a spectral graph theory for the matrix \hat{M}_R, R ...

needs_review.question_text_raw: Find a combinatorial characterization of strong cospectrality.

evidence.quote: Find a combinatorial characterization of strong cospectrality.
The standard characterization says that two vertices are strongly cospectral if and only if they are cospectral and parallel.
